title: Chapter 9: Forty One Pending
content: The service door is on the alley side, under a light with a broken cage, and Mars is already there with her keys out and her coat buttoned wrong.
"Six ten," Mars says. "You're late."
"You said six."

"I said between six and never." She puts the key in and turns it twice. "The night man does his rounds at seven and again at ten. We have forty minutes, and if he sees you I don't know you, and you're here about a dog license."
"I don't have a dog."
"Then you're here about a fence." Mars holds the door. "You're here about a fence, Wren."

The freight elevator is the size of a small room and smells of hydraulic oil. Mars presses B and the cage closes and they go down past the ground floor and keep going, and Wren watches the numbers and counts, because counting is what she does now.

The records room is cold and dry and lit in strips, and it is bigger than the diner. Shelves to the ceiling, boxes aligned, a long table in the middle with a mat and a ruler and a pencil cup. The air tastes like paper and the inside of an old book.

"Death records, 1990 forward, are on the north wall," Mars says. "The gate series is separate. It's not in the county death index, because a gate death isn't a county death until somebody certifies it, and nobody has."
"Then what is it?"
"It's a file." Mars walks her down the aisle. "It's a file that exists and doesn't count. That's a category this county invented."
The shelf is at chest height, one gray archive box, and on the end of it, in marker, in a hand that is not Mars's, somebody has written KETTLER GATE. RELEASES. HOLD.
Mars puts on cotton gloves and hands Wren a pair. "Rule," she says. "I copy things. I don't steal things. There's a difference and I'd like to keep it."
"I don't want to steal anything."
"Everybody says that in a basement." Mars lifts the lid. "You want to take something. Taking's the same as stealing except it feels better."
Inside are folders, upright, tabbed, and the tabs are uneven because they have been added to over thirty-two years by people who did not expect there to be more.
Wren counts them with one finger. She counts them twice.
"Forty-one."
"Forty-one," Mars says. "Since 1994. There's a note in the front of the box that says so, in case you think I'm making it up."
The note is a sheet of county letterhead with three lines typed on it, and the third line says: 41 to date. Somebody has written a small question mark after it in pencil and never come back to it.
Wren opens the first folder.

Owen Pike. 43. 14 May 1994. The gate released at 6:20 a.m. for silt. The folder holds a Form 9 with the cause line blank, a sheriff's report that runs to one page and a half, and a carbon of a letter from the Basin Authority saying the release was a scheduled maintenance event and that the river below the gate is a working river. Every sheet is stamped in the corner, and every stamp is the same word.
PENDING.
"Read the cause line," Mars says.
"There isn't one."
"Read what's there."

Wren turns the page. In the box marked cause, as certified, somebody has typed the word undetermined and then drawn a single line through it, and under the line, in pen, in a small neat hand, is written pending.
"Who writes that?"

"Hollis Drane, for the first eleven years. Then a woman named Betts. Then Hollis again, because Betts retired and they gave it back to him." Mars is quiet a moment. "It's a reflex. Like a man saying bless you."

Wren closes Owen Pike and opens the next folder and the next. 1995, a woman of sixty-one taken off the bank at Mile 9. 1996, two men in one folder, a boat ramp, a cooler still floating. 1997, a boy of nineteen, and in his folder there is a photograph of a boot.
She stops reading names and starts reading dates.

Every folder has a release date in it, typed or written, and every release date matches the date of death. She checks six, then twelve, then all of them, and it holds. The gate opened and somebody below it stopped.
"How many at night?" she says.
"Night?"
"After dark. What time do the releases run?"
Mars pulls the box's index sheet and runs her finger down it. "Nineteen of them. Maybe twenty. Some of the reports don't give a time."
Wren sets the folders back in order. Her hands are steady and her jaw is not.
"Twenty out of forty-one," she says. "At night. On a river with no siren."
"That's the number," Mars says. "That's the number nobody has ever put in one place before. It's in forty-one places."
Wren goes back along the row and pulls a folder at random from the middle, 2004, and opens it on the table.
Nadine Cotter. Nine. 3 August. The folder is thin, and the thinness is the thing that gets her, because a child should take more paper than that.

There is a witness statement in it, two pages, on a form with a ferry company's name printed at the top. She knows the form. It is in the drawer of the ferry house, a pad of them, blank, going yellow.
The statement is in her grandfather's hand.

I was at the landing. The water come up. The girl was on the lower bank with her mother. I went in but the current had her. I got her out at the piling. She was not breathing. I am 56 years old and I have crossed this river 40 years.
It is signed E. Aubrey, ferryman, Mile 9, and there is a line under the signature, drawn with a ruler, and the line is the only straight thing on the page.

Wren reads it three times. The word come, which he always said, which she has heard a thousand times and never once seen written down. The number forty, which was wrong, because he had crossed it twenty-nine years by then and he was never wrong about the ferry.
"He gave statements," she says.
"He gave nine of them. I checked the tabs." Mars is standing back, arms folded. "He's the witness in nine folders. Nobody ever called him as a witness in anything."
Wren photographs the statement, both pages, and then the tabs again.
The gap in the tabs.
She goes back along the row twice, then takes them out and lays them on the table in order, and the year on each tab goes 1997, then 1999, and there is nothing between them.
"You're missing 1998."
Mars looks at the table. "We're not missing it. It's not in this series."
"Was there a release in 1998?"
"There were three."
"Then where are the folders?"

Mars's face does something Wren has not seen on it before, which is caution with an edge of fear. "There's no folder. There's a boating accident in the county index, 4 July 1998, one male, and it's certified, and the certification is signed by a clerk named Drane."
"Drane."

"Hollis Drane. He was twenty-nine and he had a stamp and he used it." Mars wipes her palms on her skirt. "You understand what a certified death means in this county? It means somebody got paid. It means the estate closed. It means there's a stone with a date on it and a bank that released an account."
"So one family in thirty-two years got a stone."
"One family got a stone," Mars says, "and forty-one got a drawer."
Wren puts her finger on the seam between 1997 and 1999.
"Whose accident?"
"I didn't look." Mars says it too quickly. "I saw the year and I closed the drawer, because I know what it looks like when a thing has been made to look finished."
Wren pulls the last folder out of the box.
Elias Aubrey. 78. 12 September 2026. Form 9, filed at the Annex on the fourteenth by W. Aubrey, granddaughter. Cause, as certified: drowned, in her handwriting. In the corner, the stamp.
PENDING.
She has seen it before, in the Annex, when Hollis's pen hovered and did not come down. It looks different here, in a box, in a basement, in a row of forty others, under a light that hums.
"Look at the routing slip," Mars says.
There is a slip in the back of the folder, a half sheet, the kind that goes with a file when it moves between offices. It has three boxes on it. Received, District 4. Reviewed by. Date returned.
Received is stamped 14 SEP. Date returned is blank.
In the box marked reviewed by, in blue ballpoint, somebody has written two letters and a period.
T.M.
Wren looks at it until the letters stop being letters.
"Who is T.M.?"
"You tell me," Mars says. "You're the one who knows the engineers."

The survey is in the kitchen drawer at home, a copy she made on the reading room machine for a quarter a page. T. Marsh, PE, at the bottom of page four, and the small crossbar he puts through every seven he writes. She notices it now every time, the way she noticed the eggs written at the bottom of a grocery list in a different pen.
The light hums. Somewhere above them a cart moves in the elevator shaft and stops.
Wren takes out her phone, and Mars does not stop her, and she photographs the slip, and then the tab, and then the whole row of forty-one tabs laid out on the table like a hand of cards.
Then she takes a records request form from the pencil cup, fills in forty-one names in the space for one, and slides it across the mat.
"Stamp it," she says.
Mars looks at the form. "It's after hours. The date stamp's in the drawer and the drawer's on my desk and my desk is upstairs."
"Then go upstairs."

Mars goes. She is gone four minutes, and Wren stands in the cold room with her hands flat on the table and does not read anything else, because she has what she came for and she has learned not to take more than she can carry.
The table is cold under her palms. The forty-one folders are lined up in order and the last one has her own handwriting in it, and she does not open it again.
The stamp comes down hard. RECEIVED, 26 SEP 2026, COUNTY OF KETTLER, and Mars signs the bottom and pushes the carbon across.
"Now it's a record," Mars says. "Now the county knows you asked. That's not the same as the county knowing what you asked for, but it's a start."
Wren folds the carbon into her jacket, the one that is too big in the shoulders, and it goes into the inside pocket where her grandfather kept his license.
"Monday," she says. "I want the vault."
Mars turns off the aisle lights one bank at a time. "The vault needs a judge's signature and a reason."
"I'll have a reason."
"You'll have forty-one of them," Mars says, and holds the door.
highlight: Mars lets Wren into the records room after hours and shows her forty-one drownings filed pending since 1994.
